facts.statement: The genus Baru was first described by Willis and colleagues in 1990.
facts.quote: authority: Willis et al., 1990

facts.statement: Fossils of Baru date from the Late Oligocene to the Late Miocene.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Oligocene - Late Miocene,

facts.statement: Baru fossils have been found in the Northern Territory and Queensland.
facts.quote: Its fossils have been found from various Late Oligocene and Miocene localities from across the Northern Territory and Queensland

facts.statement: Baru had an incredibly deep and robust skull with long teeth featuring compressed crowns.
facts.quote: Baru was a large and powerful mekosuchine with an incredibly deep and robust skull and long teeth with compressed crowns

facts.statement: Baru reached a length of around 4 meters.
facts.quote: At a length of around 4 m, it was among the largest crocodilians native to Australia at the time

facts.statement: Baru is generally interpreted as a semi-aquatic ambush hunter.
facts.quote: With dorsally oriented nostrils and eyes and a poor range of head movement, as well as its fossils being associated with freshwater environments, Baru is generally interpreted to have been a semi-aquatic ambush hunter

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Baru inhabited shallower waters than modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: Willis and colleagues suggest that it inhabited shallower waters that were not suited to drown potential prey items as done by today's crocodiles

facts.statement: The bite of Baru was thought to be powerful enough to kill large mammals up to 300 kg.
facts.quote: The bite of Baru is thought to have been powerful enough to take out even large mammals up to a weight of 300 kg

facts.statement: Baru went extinct during the Late Miocene due to climate changes.
facts.quote: Although highly successful during the Oligocene and Miocene, Baru eventually fell victim to changes in Australia's climate at some point during the Late Miocene

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that a pulse of aridification destroyed the habitat preferred by Baru.
facts.quote: One hypothesis suggests that the continent was hit by an especially devastating pulse of aridification that was severe enough to destroy the habitat preferred by Baru

facts.statement: The species B. darrowi was named in 1990.
facts.quote: B. darrowi being named in 1990 on the basis of various fossils found in the Northern Territory and Queensland

facts.statement: The holotype of B. darrowi is a partial rostrum collected from Bullock Creek.
facts.quote: The holotype, a partial rostrum, was collected from the Bullock Creek Local Fauna in the Northern Territory

facts.statement: Fossil finds at the Alcoota site date back to 1962.
facts.quote: There had been fossil finds at the site predating even the description of Baru, going as far back as 1962

facts.statement: The species Baru iylwenpeny was named in 2023 based on material from the Alcoota site.
facts.quote: Furthermore, the Alcoota material is recognized as likely having belonged to a distinct species, which after initially being slated for a 2022 publication was unveiled in 2023 and given the name Baru iylwenpeny

facts.statement: The name Baru comes from a figure in the Dreamtime of the East Arnhem Region.
facts.quote: The word Baru is taken from a figure in the Dreamtime, specifically the believes held by the people of the East Arnhem Region

facts.statement: B. darrowi reached 4 meters in length and lived during the Middle Miocene.
facts.quote: It was roughly the same size as Baru wickeni, reaching 4 m in length, and much younger, dating to the Middle Miocene

facts.statement: B. iylwenpeny is noted for being more robust than other species of Baru.
facts.quote: Baru iylwenpeny is also noted for its robustness, exceeding even the other species of its genus

facts.statement: B. wickeni lived during the Late Oligocene and was described in 1997.
facts.quote: B. wickeni is the older of the two species, living during the Late Oligocene and was described by Willis in 1997

facts.statement: B. wickeni was named after Tony Wicken, a curator at the University of New South Wales.
facts.quote: Like the type species, B. wickeni was named for a supporter of the Riversleigh Research Project, specifically Tony Wicken

facts.statement: Ultrastenos is now considered closer to Mekosuchus and Trilophosuchus.
facts.quote: Ultrastenos is now thought to be closer to Mekosuchus and Trilophosuchus

facts.statement: Some researchers describe the Baru skull as altirostral, distinguishing it from the platyrostral snout shape found in generalist crocodilians like Paludirex, Kambara, and Australosuchus.
facts.quote: The skull is trapezoid in cross section and described as altirostral by some researchers, setting it apart from the platyrostral snout shape typically associated with generalist crocodilians such as Paludirex, Kambara and Australosuchus.

facts.statement: In dorsal view, the Baru skull is triangular, a shape typical for many crocodiles.
facts.quote: In dorsal view the skull is triangular, as typical for many crocodiles.

facts.statement: The Baru premaxilla is a short, wide, and robust element that matches the proportions of the rest of the skull.
facts.quote: The premaxilla, the very tip of the snout, is a short, wide and robust element matching the proportions of the rest of the skull.

facts.statement: The profile of the Baru premaxilla between the teeth and nostrils is very blunt and nearly vertical across all species.
facts.quote: However, most notable across all species is the profile of the premaxilla between the teeth and the nostrils, as it is very blunt and nearly vertical.

facts.statement: The notch at the contact between the premaxilla and maxilla gives the premaxilla a D-shape when viewed from above.
facts.quote: This notch not only marks the end of the premaxilla in side view, but also gives the element a D-shape when viewed from above.

facts.statement: In Baru darrowi, the external opening of the nares is entirely surrounded by the premaxilla.
facts.quote: In Baru darrowi it is entirely surrounded by the premaxilla.

facts.statement: In Baru wickeni and Baru iylwenpeny, the paired nasal bones contact the external nares by penetrating the upper surface of the premaxilla.
facts.quote: In contrast, the nares of Baru wickeni and Baru iylwenpeny are contacted by the paired nasal bones, which penetrate the upper surface of the premaxilla and contact the external nares.

facts.statement: The sides of the mandibular ramus of Baru are heavily sculpted.
facts.quote: The sides of the mandibular ramus of Baru is heavily sculpted.

facts.statement: On the surangular bone, the edge of the sculpted area is bordered by a ridge projecting towards the side in both Baru darrowi and Baru wickeni.
facts.quote: On the surangular bone, the edge of this sculpted area is bordered by a ridge that projects towards the side in both Baru darrowi and Baru wickeni.

facts.statement: Similar to the upper jaw, the Baru mandible displays pronounced festooning.
facts.quote: Similar to the upper jaw, the mandible displays pronounced festooning.

facts.statement: All premaxillary teeth and the first six maxillary teeth of Baru pointed backwards.
facts.quote: All teeth of the premaxilla and the first six of the maxilla are pointed backwards.

facts.statement: The front teeth of Baru had a D-shaped cross-section with a curved outer side and a flat inner side.
facts.quote: More specifically, this gives the tooth crown a more D-shaped cross section, with the side facing out being more curved and the side facing inward being flatter.

facts.statement: The rear teeth of Baru had a consistently compressed, elliptical cross-section.
facts.quote: The more posterior teeth on the other hand do not show this stark contrast in cross section between base and crown and are instead consistently compressed, giving them an elliptical cross section.

facts.statement: The front and back edges of Baru's teeth featured well-developed cutting ridges called carinae.
facts.quote: The front and back of the teeth are marked by well developed cutting edges, so called carinae.

facts.statement: The cutting edges of Baru wickeni were smooth, while those of Baru darrowi and Baru iylwenpeny had fine serrations.
facts.quote: In Baru wickeni, the older of the two species, the cutting edges are smooth. However, those of the later Baru darrowi and Baru iylwenpeny showcase minute crenulation, a kind of very fine serration.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Baru's teeth should be classified as ziphodont due to insufficient development of serrations compared to true ziphodont teeth like those of Quinkana.
facts.quote: In early research it is therefore written that Barus teeth were ziphodont, however more recent publications argue that the crenulation is not developed enough to warrant them being described as such.

facts.statement: Adult Baru had four to five teeth in each premaxilla and twelve to thirteen in each maxilla.
facts.quote: The dentition of adult Baru consists of four to five teeth in each premaxilla, followed by 12 to 13 in each maxilla.

facts.statement: The second premaxillary tooth of Baru was gradually reduced and lost entirely as the animal aged.
facts.quote: As Baru age, the second tooth of the premaxilla is gradually reduced until it is lost entirely.

facts.statement: The upper teeth of Baru overlapped the lower teeth in the front part of the jaw.
facts.quote: Reception pits for the teeth of the lower jaw are situated lingual to the teeth of the maxilla, showcasing that in this part of the jaw the upper teeth overlapped the lower teeth.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Baru contained fifteen teeth similar to those in the upper jaw.
facts.quote: The lower jaw contained 15 teeth similar to those of the upper jaw.

facts.statement: The spacing of the sixth, seventh, and eighth maxillary teeth distinguishes different species within the genus Baru.
facts.quote: Among the maxillary teeth, the sixth, seventh and eighth all serve to separate the different taxa within the genus, as the distance between them differs among the species.

facts.statement: Baru was among the larger mekosuchines, with adult skulls reaching a length of 50 cm.
facts.quote: Size Baru was among the larger mekosuchines, with the skulls of adults reaching a length of 50 cm.

facts.statement: The largest known skull of Baru iylwenpeny measured 58.8 cm.
facts.quote: In particular, Baru iylwenpeny seemingly grew larger than its older relatives, with the largest known skull measuring 58.8 cm.

facts.statement: Baru is now typically classified as a derived mekosuchine related to the semi-aquatic Paludirex.
facts.quote: Although its placement in early studies varied depending on the author, its place within the family has gradually crystalized, with it now typically being considered to be a derived mekosuchine related to the likewise semi-aquatic Paludirex.

facts.statement: A 2018 study by Lee and Yates found Baru claded with Pallimnarchus and Kalthifrons as a sister group to dwarf mekosuchines.
facts.quote: In their 2018 study, Lee and Yates utilized stratigraphic, morphological and genetic information to determine the relationships of crocodilians, finding that Baru claded with Pallimnarchus and Kalthifrons as a sister group to the dwarf mekosuchines like Trilophosuchus and Mekosuchus.

facts.statement: A recent study by Ristevski et al. grouped Baru with Paludirex and Quinkana, placing Kalthifrons as a more basal taxon.
facts.quote: A more recent study by Ristevski et al. found somewhat similar results, except that the majority of their studies recovered Kalthifrons as a more basal taxon while Baru grouped with Paludirex and Quinkana.

facts.statement: Baru's skull functioned like a cleaver, using large, closely spaced, backward-directed teeth and prominent festooning to deliver incapacitating blows to prey.
facts.quote: The large, closely spaced and backwards directed teeth combined with the prominent festooning of the jaws suggest that the skull of Baru functioned much like a cleaver, delivering a devastating and incapacitating blow to any potential prey items.

facts.statement: Willis and colleagues speculate that Baru darrowi could have taken down prey weighing up to 300 kg based on its size and build.

facts.statement: Willis suggests that Baru inhabited shallower waters than modern saltwater crocodiles, making drowning prey less effective and necessitating a faster kill.

facts.statement: Yates and colleagues note that juvenile Baru iylwenpeny had more compressed teeth than adults, with anterior teeth becoming more circular in cross-section.

facts.statement: Yates (2017) and later studies established that "Baru" huberi is not a species of Baru but belongs to the genus Ultrastenos.
facts.quote: As has been established by Yates in 2017 and confirmed by later studies, "Baru" huberi is not a species of Baru at all but a member of the genus Ultrastenos.

facts.statement: There is currently no fossil evidence linking Late Miocene Baru iylwenpeny to its likely Late Oligocene divergence time.
facts.quote: There is however at present no fossil evidence linking the Late Miocene Baru iylwenpeny to its likeliest divergence time, which was during the Late Oligocene.

facts.statement: Results from Lee and Yates (2018) suggested that Baru iylwenpeny was the sister taxon to Baru darrowi, contrasting with findings from the type description of Baru iylwenpeny.
facts.quote: This contrasts with the results of Lee and Yates 2018, in which Baru iylwenpeny, then undescribed and unnamed, was the sister taxon to Baru darrowi.
